html:
A spiritual teacher and poet of the Punjab, born in 1469, who founded Sikhism and was the first of its ten Gurus. He taught that there is one God, that all people are equal, and that a good life is lived through honest work, sharing and remembering God.

He was born at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan, into a Hindu family, and worked for a time as a storekeeper. Sikh tradition says that around the age of thirty he disappeared into a river for three days and came back saying, "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim." He then spent many years travelling, with a Muslim musician named Mardana, teaching through songs. Traditional accounts say these journeys took him across India and as far as Sri Lanka, Tibet, Mecca and Baghdad.

His core teachings:

  • God is one, without form, and present in all creation.
  • Caste, idol worship and empty ritual do not bring anyone closer to God.
  • People should earn an honest living, share with others, and keep God's name in mind.

He lived in an age of bhakti and Sufi devotion, when poets like Kabir were also rejecting the walls between faiths. He saw Babur's invasion of the Punjab, the end of the Delhi Sultanate, and wrote about its cruelty.

In his last years he settled at Kartarpur, where his followers farmed together and ate together in a shared kitchen, the langar, still found at every Sikh temple. Before he died in 1539 he chose a disciple, Angad, as his successor. His 974 hymns form the core of the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture. The later Sikh community grew into a political power, the Sikh Empire.
